method: The ring is treated as a regular n-gon: the finished outer diameter D fixes the circumradius D/2, and each segment's outer edge is the chord between two neighbouring vertices, D times sin(180 degrees divided by n). The inner edge is the same chord taken on the inner diameter, which is D minus twice the wall, so the segment is a trapezoid with parallel short and long edges. Both ends are mitered at 180 degrees divided by n from square, which makes the two cut faces of one segment meet at 180 minus 360/n degrees and lets n segments close the ring at n glue joints. Because the saw removes its kerf at every cut, the cut length is the finished outer edge plus one kerf; the strip to prepare is as wide as the ring wall and as long as the n cut lengths summed, and the kerf allowance is reported separately so offcuts can be planned. The page accepts 3 to 96 segments per ring, an outer diameter from 50 to 2000 mm, a wall from 5 to 250 mm, a kerf from 0 to 6 mm and 1 to 50 rings. A wall that leaves an inner diameter under 20 mm is refused, and so is a segment count that would leave outer edges under 8 mm, because such a piece cannot be cut or clamped. Segments under 20 mm across the outer edge, an inner edge under 5 mm, and a kerf that removes more than a tenth of the cut length each raise a warning rather than a refusal. Lengths are reported to 0.001 mm and angles to 0.0001 degrees, and decimal commas are accepted. The model assumes straight parallel miter cuts and a constant kerf; blade runout, glue-line thickness, snipe, ring stacking, the hollowing allowance and wood movement are not modelled, and the result is a cut list rather than a structural claim. The page runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Wolfram MathWorld, Regular Polygon: the side of a regular n-gon is a = 2R sin(pi/n) and its interior angle is (n-2)pi/n
Wikipedia, Segmented turning: rings are built from three or more segments joined with angled miter joints, cut to tolerances of as little as a tenth of a degree
